This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst. At least 11 people were killed in a firefight last night as
Mexican authorities captured one of the most wanted drug lords in the country.
Empirizada Peralto reports he was on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted List.
Fausto Isidro Mesaflores, who was better known as El Chapo Isidro, is the leader of the Beltran Leyva cartel.
The U.S. accuses him of running huge quantities of drugs, including meth and fentanyl, to the U.S.
The Mexican military says it captured Mesaflores in Wasave, Sinaloa, using U.S. intelligence.
Residents reported that the military fired from helicopters while the cartels burned cars and trucks.
A baseball game was disrupted by the heavy fighting and some residents had to spend the night at a supermarket to stay safe.
Over the past couple of years, as the U.S. has mounted pressure on Mexico to fight organized crime,
security forces have captured a number of drug lords. The power vacuums have often led to an increase in violence.
Eir Peralto, NPR News, Mexico City.
A new survey finds more than 4 in 10 adults in the U.S. say they've had at least one serious financial hardship in the past year.
Empiriz Jennifer Ludden reports that's the highest level in a decade.
The most common hardships? Having to borrow money from family or friends to pay bills and
not paying an important bill in full. That's according to the American Family Survey by researchers at Brigham Young University.
People also reported being hungry,
foregoing medical care, having to move in with someone else, or losing housing altogether.
The poll also finds broad concern about being able to afford a home or family.
In fact, when younger adults were asked, "What's the most important thing to do before having a child?" being financially stable topped the list.
Looking ahead, most Americans of all ages say the biggest threat to their finances is inflation.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News.
A final draft of a climate agreement at the United Nations Climate Summit in Turkey called COP 31
failed to mention the impact of fossil fuels on global warming,
leading international delegates to add another day to their deliberations.
Empiriz Rachel Waldhos has more from Antalya.
Many of the countries that have been most affected by climate change,
they want the agreement that comes out of Antalya to explicitly state that it's necessary for the world to transition away from fossil fuels and
oil-producing countries, notably Saudi Arabia and Russia,
they're resisting that language. Burning fossil fuels like coal and oil and natural gas,
it's the primary driver of climate change. It is also the key to the global economy, and so it's always a delicate issue.
Empiriz Rachel Waldhos. If countries can't reach a consensus,
negotiations could be suspended. This year's summit came after a year of deadly heat waves and floods as the war in Iran created a global
energy crisis. You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Major League Baseball players have rejected a management proposal for an international amateur draft.
Instead, they want bigger signing bonuses pools under the current system and more rewards for small market teams.
MLB's five-year contract ends at midnight December 1st, and if no agreement is met,
management is expected to lock the players out. If that happens, it will be baseball's 10th work stoppage since 1972.
There's a new effort underway in northern Minnesota to help bring back an ancient fish.
Minnesota Public Radio's Dan Crocker has more on the giant lake sturgeon.
Sturgeon are enormous fish that can live well over 100 years.
They were wiped out from the St. Louis River in the mid-1900s. For decades, biologists have worked to bring them back.
Miranda Rini with the Great Lakes Aquarium says this new approach raises baby sturgeon directly in water from the river. The sturgeon
imprint on the water they're raised on within the first 30 to 45 days of their life,
and that cues them of where to return to spawn. Earlier this month, hundreds of seven-inch-long sturgeon were released into the river.
Have a good life, little buddies. The goal is to make their populations self-sustaining. For NPR News, I'm Dan Crocker in Duluth.
Honda and Toyota are recalling around 1.6 million vehicles because the Takata airbag inflators could rupture.
Both automakers say no injuries or crashes nor airbag inflator ruptures have been reported,
but there have been at least 28 deaths of more than 400 injuries.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
